live.name: NICKEL FOXCROFT
live.headline: NICKEL FOXCROFT: a threat actor known by many names
live.in_short: The catalogue lists NICKEL FOXCROFT under many aliases, including APT37 and ScarCruft, and names eight tools tied to it. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL FOXCROFT is the Secureworks name for a threat actor tracked under many other names.
Its aliases include APT37, ATK4, Group 123, InkySquid, Moldy Pisces, Operation Daybreak, Operaton Erebus, RICOCHET CHOLLIMA, Reaper, ScarCruft, TA-RedAnt and Venus 121.
The catalogue links eight tools to the actor: Bluelight, Chinotto, GOLDBACKDOOR, KevDroid, KoSpy, PoorWeb, ROKRAT and final1stpy.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: NICKEL FOXCROFT
next.headline: NICKEL FOXCROFT (APT37, ScarCruft): a long-running espionage group focused on South Korea
next.in_short: Vendors describe NICKEL FOXCROFT, better known as APT37 or ScarCruft, as a North Korea-aligned espionage group active since at least 2012. It mainly targets South Korean officials, activists, journalists and defectors.

sentences.t: Secureworks tracks this actor as NICKEL FOXCROFT. Other names for it include APT37, ScarCruft, Reaper, Group 123, InkySquid, Moldy Pisces and RICOCHET CHOLLIMA.
ESET says ScarCruft, also known as APT37 or Reaper, has operated since at least 2012 and is suspected to be a North Korean espionage group.
CrowdStrike calls its RICOCHET CHOLLIMA profile a North Korea-nexus targeted intrusion adversary. It says the group has run espionage operations since at least 2016.

Genians says the KONNI activity overlaps with Kimsuky and APT37 in targets and infrastructure, so some researchers treat them as one group. Genians also cites the MSMT report, which assesses Kimsuky and KONNI as distinct groups.
CrowdStrike says the group's observed operations have almost exclusively targeted South Korea. It assesses the focus to be government officials, NGOs, academics and journalists.
AhnLab's ASEC says the group targets individuals such as human rights activists, reporters and North Korean defectors.
Genians reports a March 2025 spear phishing campaign by APT37 against activists focused on North Korea.
China's 360 Advanced Threat Research Institute says a RokRat campaign targeted government personnel and corporations in South Korea and across Asia.
ESET infers that a game-platform attack in the Yanbian region of China was aimed at ethnic Koreans there, most likely refugees or defectors.
Zscaler says APT37 has used Windows shortcut (LNK) files as an initial way in for years.

One analysis of the RokRat backdoor describes phishing emails with ZIP files holding hidden shortcuts. These start a PowerShell chain that loads the payload in memory. RokRat then uses pCloud, Yandex and Dropbox for command and control.
360 says RokRat has been the group's main remote access tool since 2016. It says the 2024 version adds anti-forensic cleanup and process hollowing.

ASEC reports an attack using an old flaw in the Hangul word processor, CVE-2017-8291. The payload was hidden inside a JPEG image and led to a backdoor called M2RAT, which logs keystrokes and takes screenshots.

Lookout attributes the KoSpy Android spyware to ScarCruft with medium confidence. The apps posed as utilities and were distributed through Google Play and Firebase Firestore. Lookout notes that North Korean groups share infrastructure and techniques, which makes attribution harder.

In 2021, S2W described a December 2020 watering-hole attack that delivered a ROKRAT variant. S2W judges from technique analysis that it relates to ScarCruft. It calls this a judgement, not a confirmed attribution.
ASEC says the M2RAT phishing attacks it observed began in January 2023.
Genians named the March 2025 campaign Operation ToyBox Story. Lures impersonated a South Korean national security think tank, and malicious shortcut files delivered the RoKRAT malware.

ESET says ScarCruft trojanized Windows and Android parts of a video game platform serving Yanbian, China. ESET says the attack was probably ongoing since late 2024 and delivered the Android BirdCall backdoor.

Zscaler's Ruby Jumper report describes an APT37 campaign that spreads through removable media to reach air-gapped networks. Zscaler says that, to its knowledge, this is the first time APT37 has abused Zoho WorkDrive.
Zscaler also describes APT37 chains that drop the Rustonotto and Chinotto backdoors. A later stage delivers FadeStealer, which collects files, keystrokes, screenshots and audio.
Treat shortcut files inside archives, and unexpected document attachments, as suspect. This matters most for people who work on North Korea-related topics.
